blocks.h: This chapter is the companion examination guide to the main body of this book. It is designed to serve three groups of readers:
• Students preparing for CIIN Foundation, Diploma, or Associateship examinations who want to understand how the content of this book maps to the CIIN syllabus.
• Practitioners who hold CIIN qualifications and are fulfilling their CPD requirements, seeking a structured development framework.
• Employers and training managers designing qualification pathways and study programmes for insurance staff.

blocks.text: 38.1 Introduction: The CIIN Qualification as Professional Credential and Regulatory Requirement

blocks.h: The Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (CIIN) qualification framework is simultaneously a professional credential and a regulatory requirement. Under the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act 2025 (NIIRA 2025), a valid CIIN qualification is required for every individual who sells insurance products in Nigeria (minimum: the Certificate of Proficiency), for key management officers including Heads of Underwriting, Claims, and Financial Planning (minimum: Associateship), and is a strong expectation for senior leadership. The qualification is therefore not optional for a serious insurance career in Nigeria — it is the professional floor.

But the CIIN qualification is also more than a compliance requirement. The knowledge embedded in the CIIN examination syllabus — insurance principles, underwriting, claims management, reinsurance, actuarial concepts, distribution, regulation, corporate governance — is the professional knowledge required to do the job well, not merely to satisfy a licensing threshold. A claims manager who understands the principles behind the claims management framework makes better decisions than one who knows only the procedures. An agent who understands why insurers need accurate disclosure makes more credible conversations with prospects than one who simply follows the proposal form prompts.

This chapter sets out the complete examination preparation framework: the qualification structure, examination formats, examination technique, the syllabus mapping to this book’s chapters, the highest-frequency examination topics, model answers to representative questions, and the CPD framework that continues professional development after qualification is achieved.

rows: Certificate of Proficiency (Cert. COP) and Certificate in Insurance (Cert. CIIN)

Entry-level professional qualification confirming basic insurance knowledge, product understanding, and regulatory awareness. Cert. COP is specifically designed for insurance sales agents; Cert. CIIN is the broader certificate qualification.
NIIRA 2025 mandates that every agent selling insurance in Nigeria holds a valid Cert. COP. This is the minimum licensing requirement for insurance distribution.

Intermediate professional qualification covering the technical core of insurance practice: underwriting, claims, reinsurance, distribution, and risk management at a level appropriate for supervisory and specialist roles.
Required for individuals progressing toward regulated functional head roles. A strong expectation for agents seeking to move into management, underwriting, or claims assessment roles.
Associate of the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (ACIIN)

The primary professional designation in Nigerian insurance. Demonstrates comprehensive mastery of insurance practice across all domains — technical, commercial, regulatory, and governance. Required for Heads of Underwriting, Claims, and Financial Planning under NIIRA 2025.
NIIRA 2025 specifies Associateship (or equivalent) as the minimum professional qualification for key functional heads in licensed Nigerian insurers.
Fellow of the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria (FCIIN)

The highest CIIN designation, recognising distinguished achievement in the insurance profession. Awarded on completion of the Fellowship examination or by distinction to practitioners of exceptional professional standing.
Strongly preferred for MD/CEO and Board-level roles in licensed Nigerian insurers. Marks a practitioner as a leader of the profession, not merely a qualified member.

blocks.h: The CIIN qualification pathway is sequential: each level builds on the knowledge base of the preceding level. A candidate cannot sit Diploma papers before completing the Foundation level, and cannot sit Associateship papers before completing the Diploma level. This sequential structure ensures that each level’s examination tests not merely the specific syllabus content of that level but the candidate’s ability to integrate prior knowledge with new material.
Typical completion timeframes (for a motivated, employed candidate studying part-time):

items.h: Certificate of Proficiency (Cert. COP): 3–6 months of part-time study; one to two examination sittings.
Certificate in Insurance (Cert. CIIN): 6–12 months of part-time study; sequential papers over two to three sittings.
Diploma in Insurance (Dip. CIIN): 12–24 months of part-time study following Foundation completion; four to six papers over multiple sittings.
Associateship (ACIIN): 24–36 months of part-time study following Diploma completion; four to six advanced papers.
Fellowship (FCIIN): Typically 12–18 months of advanced study following Associateship; two to three senior-level papers or special assessment.

blocks.h: CIIN examinations are conducted in defined ‘diets’ — scheduled sitting periods throughout the year. CIIN typically conducts at least two major examination diets per year, with a possible third for specific papers:

rows: The primary mid-year examination sitting. Most papers across all qualification levels are available. Results are typically published 6–8 weeks after the examination date.

The primary end-year examination sitting. All papers available. Results published in December or January. This is often the preferred sitting for candidates who began studying in the first half of the year.

CIIN sometimes schedules a March sitting for selected Foundation and Diploma papers to provide an additional opportunity for candidates who missed the May/June diet or who are on accelerated pathways.

blocks.h: REGISTRATION DEADLINE: Typically 8–10 weeks before the examination date. Late registration may be permitted with a surcharge, but closes 4 weeks before the sitting. Candidates registering late risk not receiving study materials in time for adequate preparation.

EXAMINATION CENTRES: CIIN conducts examinations at approved examination centres in Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, Kano, Enugu, and other state capitals. Candidates select their preferred centre at registration. International centres may be available for diaspora candidates on request.

EXAMINATION DAY REQUIREMENTS: Valid government-issued identification (NIN slip, international passport, or national ID card); CIIN candidate number; approved stationery. Electronic devices (including mobile phones and calculators unless specifically permitted) are prohibited.

RESULTS AND TRANSCRIPTS: Results are published on the CIIN portal (ciin.org.ng) within the stated result release period. Official transcripts and certificates are issued by the CIIN Examinations department on request. Employers requiring verification of qualifications should request a CIIN verification letter directly from CIIN.

CIIN examinations use three primary question formats across the qualification levels. Understanding the format of each paper — and the specific skills each format tests — is essential to effective preparation. A candidate who prepares comprehensively for the content but does not understand the format of the examination they are sitting will underperform relative to their actual knowledge level.

MCQ papers are used primarily at the Foundation (Cert. COP and Cert. CIIN) level and for some Diploma papers. Each question presents a stem (the question or incomplete statement) followed by four options (A, B, C, D), of which exactly one is correct. The remaining three options are distractors — plausible but incorrect answers designed to identify candidates with imprecise or incomplete knowledge.

blocks.title: How MCQ Distractors Work: An Example

blocks.h: Question: The doctrine of utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei) in insurance requires:
(A) The insurer to pay all claims within 60 days of notification.
(B) Both parties to the insurance contract to disclose all material facts honestly and completely.
(C) The policyholder to pay premiums on time without a grace period.
(D) The insurer to provide coverage for all risks disclosed at application.

Analysis: (B) is correct. (A) describes a regulatory claims settlement requirement, not the uberrimae fidei doctrine. (C) confuses premium payment obligations with the disclosure duty. (D) inverts the doctrine — disclosure does not create an obligation to cover all disclosed risks. All three distractors contain a kernel of insurance truth, making them plausible to a candidate with superficial knowledge.

MCQ examination technique: read the stem carefully before reading the options; answer the question in your head before looking at the options to avoid being influenced by plausible distractors; eliminate options you know are wrong before selecting from the remaining options; do not leave any question unanswered (there is no penalty for incorrect answers in most CIIN MCQ formats — confirm this at registration); manage time to complete all questions (allow approximately 1.5 minutes per MCQ question).

At Diploma level, CIIN papers typically use structured questions requiring written answers of defined length — from one-sentence definitions to multi-paragraph explanations. Structured questions may be subdivided into parts (a), (b), (c) with different command words and mark allocations. The mark allocation for each part should guide the length and depth of the response: a 2-mark question requires a 2-sentence answer; a 10-mark question requires a substantive response across several paragraphs.

Structured question technique: read the full question before starting to write; note the mark allocation for each part and apportion your time accordingly; use the command word (define, describe, explain, identify, distinguish) as a guide to the required format; use brief subheadings or clear paragraph breaks to make your structure visible to the examiner; do not write more than the marks justify.

At Associateship level, CIIN papers include extended essay questions requiring a sustained, well-structured analytical response. Essay questions typically use higher-order command words: ‘critically evaluate’, ‘analyse’, ‘assess’, ‘compare and contrast’, ‘to what extent’. These command words signal that the examiner is looking not merely for knowledge recall but for analytical thinking, evidence-based argument, and the ability to take and defend a position.

blocks.title: Anatomy of a High-Scoring Associateship Essay Answer

blocks.h: INTRODUCTION (10–15% of response): Frame the question in your own words. Define key terms. State the argument or position you will develop. Do not pad the introduction with general statements that add no analytical value.

BODY (70–80% of response): Develop the argument in clearly structured paragraphs, each with a clear topic sentence. Use specific examples, regulatory provisions, and data where available to support each point. Address both sides of an evaluative question — an essay that argues only one side of a ‘critically evaluate’ question will score in the middle range even if technically accurate.

CONCLUSION (10–15% of response): Summarise the key argument without merely repeating the body’s points. State a clear, evidence-based conclusion. For evaluative questions, state your overall judgement and the principal reasons for it.

WHAT MARKS ARE AWARDED FOR: Knowledge and understanding of relevant concepts (typically 40% of marks); analysis and application to the specific question (typically 35%); evaluation, judgement, and conclusion (typically 25%). Candidates who demonstrate knowledge but do not apply it to the specific question consistently score in the 45–55% range, regardless of their technical knowledge level.

At Associateship level, some papers include case study questions presenting a detailed description of a company, situation, or problem, followed by several related sub-questions that require the candidate to apply their knowledge to the specific case. Case study questions require a different approach from pure essay questions:

items.h: Read the case carefully before reading the questions, making brief notes on the key facts, issues, and characteristics of the case as you read.

Identify the specific facts in the case that are relevant to each sub-question — case study marks are awarded for applying knowledge to the specific case facts, not for describing general principles without reference to the case.

Organise your answer to follow the sub-question structure exactly; do not write a single discursive essay that addresses all sub-questions without clearly identifying which part of your answer corresponds to which sub-question.
Use the mark allocation to guide the depth of each sub-answer; a 5-mark sub-question within a case study requires a shorter response than a 20-mark sub-question.

blocks.h: The command word is the most important word in any examination question. It tells the candidate exactly what type of response is expected. The most common failure mode in CIIN examinations is to provide the wrong type of response — typically, a descriptive response to an evaluative question, or a general response to a specific application question. The following command word guide should be memorised:

rows: A precise, concise statement of the meaning of a term. Typically 1–2 sentences maximum.
Describing rather than defining. Giving an example instead of a definition.
List or name the specified items without extended explanation. Bullet points are appropriate.
Writing explanatory paragraphs when a list is sufficient. Identifying fewer items than requested.
A detailed account of a concept, process, product, or characteristic. More depth than ‘identify’; full sentences required.
Listing without description (treating ‘describe’ as ‘identify’). Describing only partially.
A clear, logical account of how or why something works, happens, or is significant. Cause-and-effect reasoning is expected.
Describing without explaining why. Providing a definition without the logical mechanism.
Identify the differences (and sometimes similarities) between two or more terms or concepts.
Describing each item separately without explicitly stating the difference between them.
Break the topic into its component parts and examine each in detail, exploring the relationships between parts.
Describing without analysing. Failing to examine how components interact.
Make a reasoned judgement about the value, importance, effectiveness, or implications of something, based on evidence.
Describing rather than evaluating. Listing points without taking a position. One-sided evaluation.
As ‘evaluate’, but explicitly requires examination of both supporting and opposing evidence before reaching a balanced, evidence-based conclusion.
Arguing only one side. Failing to reach a clear conclusion. Treating as ‘describe’.
Identify both similarities and differences between two or more items in a structured way.
Addressing only differences and ignoring similarities, or vice versa.
A balanced consideration of multiple aspects or perspectives on a topic, typically arriving at a conclusion.
Presenting only one perspective. Listing points without developing them into a discussion.
A structured summary without full detail; more than ‘identify’ but less depth than ‘describe’.
Writing as much as a ‘describe’ answer (wasting time) or as little as an ‘identify’ list.
Make and justify a specific course of action based on the facts of the question; your recommendation must be reasoned, not merely stated.
Describing options without making a clear recommendation. Recommending without justification.

blocks.h: Based on the structure of the CIIN syllabus and the core knowledge requirements at each level, the following topics appear most frequently in examination papers and carry the highest aggregate mark weight. Candidates should ensure they have deep and reliable knowledge of these topics before turning to lower-frequency areas.

blocks.title: Cert. COP / Cert. CIIN: Must-Know Topics

blocks.h: INSURANCE PRINCIPLES: Insurable interest (definition, examples in life insurance); utmost good faith (mutual obligation on both parties); disclosure and non-disclosure (what constitutes a material fact; consequences of non-disclosure); indemnity (why life insurance is not an indemnity contract); the distinction between pure risk and speculative risk.

LIFE ASSURANCE PRODUCTS: Term assurance (level, decreasing, convertible, renewable); whole life (participating and non-participating); endowment (savings and protection combination); unit-linked products (investment risk lies with policyholder); group life (employer obligation under PRA 2014, free cover limit, census); annuities (immediate vs. deferred, level vs. escalating).

REGULATORY FRAMEWORK: NAICOM’s role and powers under NIIRA 2025; CIIN qualification requirements for agents; the no-premium-no-cover principle; mandatory insurance (group life 3× annual salary under PRA 2014, TPMI); NDPA 2023 data protection basics for insurance.

DISTRIBUTION AND AGENCY: The role of the tied agent; the role of the insurance broker (acts for the client, not the insurer); the NIGO (Not In Good Order) application and its consequences; NIIRA 2025 commission guidelines; the persistency rate and its significance.

ETHICS AND MARKET CONDUCT: The suitability requirement; mis-selling (definition, consequences, prevention); the duty of confidentiality to policyholders; the treating customers fairly (TCF) principle; AML/KYC obligations for agents.

UNDERWRITING: The underwriting process for individual and group life; the free cover limit and its actuarial rationale; types of evidence required (medical examination, blood tests, HIV testing thresholds); premium loading and exclusion as alternatives to decline; the reinsurance retention limit and its relationship to underwriting capacity; financial underwriting and over-insurance prevention.

CLAIMS MANAGEMENT: The NIIRA 2025 mandatory claims settlement timeline; the claims documentation requirements for death claims, disability claims, and critical illness claims; fraudulent claims indicators and the Special Investigation Unit; the difference between repudiation and contestation; handling competing beneficiary claims.

REINSURANCE: Quota share vs. surplus treaty (proportional); excess of loss — risk and catastrophe (non-proportional); the domestic cession requirement under NIIRA 2025; facultative vs. automatic treaty placement; reinsurance commission; the retention limit and its determinants.

RISK MANAGEMENT: The Enterprise Risk Management framework; the four insurance risk categories (mortality, morbidity, longevity, lapse); the ORSA and its components; the three lines of defence model; stress testing and scenario analysis.

CORPORATE GOVERNANCE: Board composition under NIIRA 2025; Board committee structure (Audit, Risk, Investment, Remuneration); the Delegation of Authority; the three lines of defence; the Statutory Actuary’s role and independence requirement; solvency margin and Risk-Based Capital.

blocks.title: Associateship: Must-Know Topics for Essay and Case Study Questions

blocks.h: STRATEGY AND COMPETITIVE DYNAMICS: Porter’s Five Forces applied to the Nigerian insurance market; the Balanced Scorecard framework; the product innovation six-gate process; competitive intelligence methods and ethical limits; embedded value and its components (ANAV, VIF, NBV); profit source analysis (C1–C4).

NIIRA 2025 ADVANCED PROVISIONS: The Risk-Based Capital framework; Insurtech licensing (Partnering Insurtech ₦10m; Standalone Insurtech ₦1–1.5bn); the regulatory sandbox; the enhanced consumer protection framework; product approval requirements; market conduct inspection powers.

DIGITAL AND INSURTECH: The full-stack vs. partnering Insurtech model distinction; embedded insurance (legal ownership, distribution, claims); parametric insurance trigger design; AI/ML model risk in underwriting; NDPA 2023 compliance for data-driven insurance; the regulatory sandbox testing framework.

ALM AND INVESTMENT: Asset-liability matching for long-duration life and annuity business; duration gap management; NAICOM admissible asset framework; investment policy statement governance; the ALCO structure and decision-making process.

HUMAN CAPITAL AND ORGANISATION: The three-lines-of-defence model in practice; the Statutory Actuary’s board independence requirement; the CRO’s governance role; performance management KPIs by role; succession planning for regulated roles; CIIN CPD requirements and employer obligations.

The following model answers demonstrate the standard expected at each CIIN level. They are ‘model’ answers in the sense that they represent a high-quality response — not necessarily a perfect maximum-marks answer, which may require more detail. Candidates should study these answers for structure and approach, not to memorise the content verbatim.

blocks.title: Foundation MCQ — Analysis of Correct and Incorrect Options

blocks.h: Question: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, an employer with 10 or more employees must provide group life insurance for each employee at a minimum sum assured of:
(A) 2× the employee’s annual basic salary.
(B) 3× the employee’s total annual emoluments.
(C) ₦5,000,000, regardless of the employee’s salary level.
(D) The employee’s total annual emoluments, including all allowances.
Correct Answer: (B)

Why (B) is correct: Section 4 of the Pension Reform Act 2014 requires a minimum group life benefit of 3× the employee’s total annual emoluments (which is broader than ‘basic salary’ alone, including allowances). This is a mandatory requirement that has been a significant driver of the Nigerian group life market.
Why (A) is wrong: 2× is the wrong multiplier, and ‘basic salary’ is the wrong base — the Act specifies total annual emoluments.
Why (C) is wrong: The Act does not specify a fixed sum; the benefit is salary-linked.
Why (D) is wrong: 1× total annual emoluments is insufficient; the Act requires 3×.

blocks.text: 38.8.2 Diploma Level — Structured Question Model Answer

blocks.h: A life insurance company is reviewing its underwriting process for individual life policies. (a) Explain the difference between a standard risk and a substandard risk in life insurance underwriting. (4 marks) (b) Describe three types of evidence an underwriter may request from an applicant presenting a substandard health history. (6 marks) (c) For each of the three evidence types in (b), explain what the evidence reveals to the underwriter that enables an informed acceptance decision. (10 marks)
(a) Standard risk vs. substandard risk (4 marks):

A standard risk is an applicant whose mortality risk profile falls within the normal parameters assumed in the insurer’s standard premium rates. The underwriter accepts the application without loading or exclusion. A substandard risk is one whose mortality risk is higher than standard due to health conditions, occupation, lifestyle, or other factors, and who must be accepted at a higher premium rate (rated), with specific exclusions, or declined. The distinction determines the terms on which the insurer will provide coverage.
(b) Three evidence types for substandard health history (6 marks):

1. Confidential Medical Attendant’s Report (CMAR): A report from the applicant’s own doctor providing their medical history, current conditions, treatment, and the doctor’s clinical opinion on the applicant’s health status.

2. Medical Examination: A clinical examination by a NAICOM-approved medical examiner, including blood pressure, height/weight (BMI), urine analysis, and other clinical measurements relevant to the underwriting assessment.

3. Specialist’s Report: A report from a specialist physician (cardiologist, oncologist, neurologist) providing a detailed clinical assessment of the specific condition disclosed, its severity, treatment, prognosis, and expected impact on life expectancy.
(c) What each evidence type reveals to the underwriter (10 marks):

1. CMAR: Reveals the complete medical history the applicant’s own doctor has recorded, potentially including conditions not mentioned on the proposal form. The CMAR provides an independent verification of the applicant’s self-reported health history and may reveal treatment records, hospital admissions, or previous diagnoses that contradict the proposal form’s disclosures. It also provides the GP’s clinical opinion on current health status and the likelihood of the condition affecting life expectancy.

2. Medical Examination: Enables the underwriter to assess the applicant’s current physical condition objectively — not through self-report but through clinical measurement. Blood pressure readings indicate cardiovascular risk; BMI reveals obesity-related mortality risk; urine analysis may indicate diabetes or kidney disease. The medical examination catches conditions that the applicant may not know they have or may have failed to disclose.

3. Specialist’s Report: Provides the specific clinical detail required to apply the actuarial mortality tables’ substandard rating tables for the disclosed condition. For example, a cardiologist’s report on an applicant with previous heart disease would quantify the current cardiac function, describe the treatment received, state the prognosis, and enable the underwriter to apply the appropriate extra mortality loading or exclusion to the policy. Without a specialist’s report, the underwriter cannot distinguish between a well-controlled low-risk condition and an uncontrolled high-risk one.

blocks.text: 38.8.3 Associateship Level — Essay Question Model Answer

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025’s introduction of Risk-Based Capital (RBC) represents a fundamental shift in the Nigerian insurance regulatory framework, replacing the traditional fixed-percentage solvency margin approach. Critically evaluate whether RBC is likely to strengthen the long-term financial soundness of Nigerian life insurers, or whether the reform’s benefits will be undermined by the industry’s current implementation capacity constraints.

blocks.title: Model Answer (Associateship Level — essay, approximately 45 minutes)

blocks.h: INTRODUCTION:

The transition from a fixed-percentage solvency margin to Risk-Based Capital (RBC) under NIIRA 2025 represents the most significant change in Nigerian insurance solvency regulation since the recapitalisation exercise of the mid-2000s. Under RBC, an insurer’s minimum capital requirement is linked to its specific risk profile rather than to a fixed percentage of premium income, incentivising better risk management and more efficient capital allocation. This essay evaluates both the theoretical case for RBC’s contribution to financial soundness and the practical implementation challenges that may limit those benefits in the Nigerian context.
THE CASE FOR RBC’S STRENGTHENING EFFECT:

The theoretical basis for RBC’s superiority over fixed-percentage solvency margins is well-established in insurance regulation globally. Fixed margins treat all insurers identically regardless of their risk profile: an insurer writing conservative long-term endowment policies requires the same regulatory capital percentage as one writing high-sum-assured medical products with significant catastrophe exposure, which is actuarially unsound. RBC addresses this by aligning the capital requirement to the actual risk — insurance risk, market risk, credit risk, operational risk — that each specific insurer carries. In principle, this creates three reinforcing benefits: insurers with well-managed risk profiles face lower capital costs, incentivising better risk management; the industry’s aggregate capital is more efficiently allocated; and systemic risks — concentrations of undercapitalised risk — are more visible to the regulator.
IMPLEMENTATION CAPACITY CONSTRAINTS:

Against these theoretical benefits must be weighed the implementation realities of the Nigerian market. RBC requires each insurer to develop internal risk models that quantify their specific risk exposures with actuarial precision — a capability that many Nigerian insurers, particularly smaller and mid-size companies, currently lack. The shortage of qualified actuaries in Nigeria is acute: the market requires far more actuarial capability than the IAN and IFoA pipelines are currently supplying. An insurer without a competent actuarial team cannot develop a credible internal risk model, meaning that NAICOM’s standardised RBC formula — rather than an insurer-specific model — will in practice determine the capital requirement for most Nigerian companies. A standardised RBC formula, while better than a fixed percentage, does not capture the risk-specificity that is RBC’s primary advantage.
ADDITIONAL CONSTRAINTS:

Data quality is a second constraint. RBC models depend on historical loss data, market risk data, and operational risk data to calibrate the risk factors. Many Nigerian insurers have incomplete or unreliable historical data — a legacy of inadequate record-keeping systems and policy lapses that make portfolios difficult to analyse. Without reliable data, even a well-designed RBC model produces unreliable capital requirements. Third, NAICOM’s own supervisory capacity to validate internal models and assess the appropriateness of RBC calculations is still developing; the risk is that RBC compliance becomes a paperwork exercise rather than a genuine reflection of each insurer’s risk position.
CONCLUSION:

RBC is a structurally superior framework to fixed-percentage solvency margins and, in the long term, is likely to strengthen Nigerian life insurers’ financial soundness. However, the benefits will not be immediate or uniform. Larger insurers with actuarial resources and good data will benefit from more efficient capital allocation relatively quickly. Smaller insurers constrained by the standardised formula, poor data quality, and limited actuarial capability will achieve compliance without achieving the risk-management quality improvement that RBC is designed to drive. The pace at which NIIRA 2025’s RBC provisions strengthen the Nigerian market will therefore depend critically on parallel investments in actuarial talent development, data infrastructure, and NAICOM’s supervisory capacity — none of which are addressed by the regulatory provision itself.

blocks.text: 38.9 How to Use This Book: A Study Plan by Qualification Level
38.9.1 Certificate of Proficiency (Cert. COP) Study Plan

rows: Read Chapters 1–5 (if available in the foundational Part One of this work) and Chapter 21 (Market Conduct, Ethics, and Consumer Protection). Focus: insurance principles, key definitions, regulatory requirements for agents.

Read Chapters 9–10 (life assurance products) and Chapter 30 (group life). Focus: understanding what each product does, its key features, and its target customer. Build a one-page product summary for each.
Read Chapters 16–17 (distribution) and Chapter 33 (pension products — CPS section only). Focus: the agent’s role, suitability obligations, CIIN qualification requirements, AML/KYC.

Complete all MCQ practice questions at Foundation level throughout this book. Identify weak areas and return to the relevant chapters. Take at least one timed mock examination under examination conditions.
Use Chapter 37 (Glossary) daily — test yourself on 10 terms each day. Review Chapter 38.5 (command words) before the examination sitting.

blocks.text: 38.9.2 Diploma in Insurance (Dip. CIIN) Study Plan

rows: Deep study of Chapters 11 (Underwriting), 12 (Claims), 13 (Actuarial Concepts — non-actuarial level), and 14 (Reinsurance). These chapters form the technical backbone of the Diploma-level examination.
Study Chapters 15 (ERM), 23 (Investment and ALM), and 24 (Corporate Governance and Solvency). Build your knowledge of the three lines of defence, ORSA, and the Board’s risk governance role.
Study Chapters 16–19 (distribution channels) and 30–33 (Group Life, Annuities, Health, Pension). Focus on connecting product design with distribution strategy.
Complete all Diploma-level practice questions in this book. Write at least two full structured question answers per week under timed conditions. Focus on command word execution.
Read NAICOM and NIA publications monthly to maintain current market awareness. The Diploma examination rewards candidates who apply regulatory context to their answers.

Intensive study of Chapters 26 (Revenue Architecture and Embedded Value), 27 (Strategy and Research), 28 (Insurtech), and 15 (ERM — ORSA and RBC). At Associateship level, you are expected to integrate across these domains.

Study Chapters 34–36 (Part Seven: The Life Insurance Enterprise). These chapters are heavily exam-weighted at Associateship level because they require the integrative thinking that distinguishes Associateship from Diploma knowledge.
Write at least one full essay answer per week. Focus on Associateship command words: critically evaluate, analyse, assess. Use the model answer in Section 38.8.3 as a structural benchmark.
Attempt full past papers under timed conditions. Develop the ability to draw on multiple chapters in a single essay response — the hallmark of Associateship-level thinking.
Practice identifying the specific facts in a case study that are relevant to each sub-question. The most common Associateship failure is providing general answers to case-specific questions.

blocks.text: 38.10 Continuing Professional Development (CPD): Requirements and Recording

blocks.h: The CIIN qualification is not the end of professional development — it is its beginning. The CPD framework ensures that qualified insurance professionals maintain and expand their knowledge throughout their active careers in a rapidly changing regulatory, product, and technology environment. CPD compliance is both a professional obligation and, under NIIRA 2025, a regulatory requirement: NAICOM market conduct inspections review CPD compliance records for key staff.

rows: 30 CPD hours per year. Minimum 15 hours (50%) must be structured CPD from approved activities. Maximum 15 hours may be unstructured CPD (self-directed reading, peer learning, mentoring).
20 CPD hours per year. Minimum 10 hours structured. Maximum 10 hours unstructured.
Specific CPD hours as determined by CIIN for the annual licence renewal cycle. Confirm current requirements at registration.
The CPD year typically runs from 1 January to 31 December. CPD records must be maintained for a minimum of 3 years and must be available for production within 30 days of a CIIN audit request.
Attendance at the CIIN Annual Conference and any CIIN-organised seminars, workshops, or webinars. CPD hours are confirmed on the CIIN Certificate of Attendance issued to each participant.
Attendance at training programmes from providers approved by CIIN for CPD purposes. The training must have a defined learning outcome relevant to insurance practice.
Formal insurance or professional skills courses with documented learning objectives and an assessment component. CIIN-accredited online learning platforms are a primary source.
Structured study for CIIN examinations at a higher level than already held qualifies as structured CPD — it is documented, outcome-focused professional development.
NAICOM, PenCom, NHIA, and CBN-organised industry training events and regulatory briefings relevant to insurance practice.
Delivering a technical presentation at a CIIN event, an NIA committee meeting, or another approved forum qualifies as structured CPD (typically half of the presentation duration).

blocks.h: The CPD record is the member’s personal responsibility. The CIIN provides a standard CPD record template (available on the CIIN portal) which each member must complete for each CPD activity:

items.h: Date, venue, and name of the CPD activity.
The learning provider and the CPD category (structured or unstructured).
Duration in hours (rounded to the nearest half-hour).
A brief statement of the learning outcome — what the member learned or applied as a result of the activity.
Documentary evidence reference: the certificate of attendance number, the training provider’s registration, or the programme brochure.

blocks.h: Employers are not directly responsible for their employees’ CIIN membership or CPD compliance — these are individual professional obligations. However, best-practice employers actively facilitate CPD through: full sponsorship of CIIN examination fees; payment for approved external training programmes; designation of specific time for CIIN Annual Conference attendance; a mandatory internal training calendar that generates structured CPD credit hours; and a quarterly CPD status check conducted by the HR function.

An employer whose professional staff consistently fail to meet CPD requirements is an employer that is not investing in professional development. The resulting competence gap is a commercial risk — underqualified staff make poorer underwriting, claims, and advisory decisions — as well as a regulatory risk under NIIRA 2025.

blocks.title: The Single Most Important Examination Preparation Habit

blocks.h: Write. Not read, not highlight, not summarise into notes. Write full answers to past questions under timed conditions, then compare your response to the model answer and identify the specific gaps. A candidate who has read every chapter of this book but has never written a timed examination answer under conditions approximating the real examination will underperform relative to their knowledge level. The examination rewards the ability to retrieve, organise, and apply knowledge under time pressure — a skill that reading develops only partially. Writing develops it fully.
